content: 1. A rapid test for detecting antibodies to the hepatitis C virus was evaluated and published in the American Journal of Gastroenterology in 2001, highlighting its diagnostic utility. 2. Lee et al. conducted a multi-center evaluation of a novel rapid test for detecting HCV infection using whole blood, serum, plasma, and oral fluid, with findings presented in the Journal of Hepatology in 2010. 3. Larrat et al. assessed the performance of a combined antigen-antibody assay for hepatitis C virus testing without the need for venipuncture, as published in the Journal of Clinical Virology in 2012. 4. Smith et al. evaluated the performance of premarket rapid HCV antibody assays across four national HIV behavioral surveillance system sites, with results published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2011. 5. Mullis et al. reported a high frequency of false-positive HCV enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay results in Rakai, Uganda, as detailed in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2013. 6. Barreto et al. performed a cost-effectiveness analysis of various diagnostic algorithms for hepatitis C virus infection, with findings published in the Brazilian Journal of Medical and Biological Research in 2008. 7. Bonacini et al. explored the impact of coexisting HIV-1 infection on the diagnosis and evaluation of hepatitis C virus, as published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2001. 8. George et al. investigated HCV viremia in HIV-infected individuals with negative HCV antibody tests, with results published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2002. 9. Thio et al. examined the screening of hepatitis C virus in HIV-infected individuals, with findings published in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology in 2000. 10. Thomson et al. studied the delayed anti-HCV antibody response in HIV-positive men acutely infected with HCV, as published in AIDS in 2009. 11. Lok and McMahon provided an update on chronic hepatitis B management in 2009, as detailed in Hepatology. 12. Brunetto et al. demonstrated that hepatitis B surface antigen serum levels can distinguish active from inactive HBV genotype D carriers, as published in Gastroenterology in 2010. 13. Chen et al. discussed long-term outcomes in hepatitis B based on the REVEAL-HBV study, as published in Clinical Liver Disease in 2007. 14. Gerlach et al. reported high rates of both spontaneous and treatment-induced viral clearance in acute hepatitis C, as published in Gastroenterology in 2003. 15. UNITAID provided a comprehensive overview of hepatitis C diagnostic technologies in a report accessed in February 2017. 16. Tanaka et al. measured serum levels of HCV core protein in patients with chronic hepatitis C treated with interferon alfa, as published in Hepatology in 1996. 17. Tillmann reviewed the role of HCV core antigen testing in diagnosis, disease monitoring, and treatment, as published in the World Journal of Gastroenterology in 2014. 18. Freiman et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on HCV core antigen testing for diagnosing HCV infection, as published in the Annals of Internal Medicine in 2016. 19. Lee et al. evaluated qualitative and quantitative AMPLICOR reverse transcription-PCR tests for HCV RNA, focusing on calibration to international units and enhanced genotype reactivity, as published in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology in 2000. 20. Yu et al. assessed the performance of HCV core antigen as an early and strong predictor of sustained virological response in genotype 1 HCV infection, as published in BMC Gastroenterology in 2014. 21. Moscato et al. explored the quantitative determination of HCV core antigen for therapy monitoring in chronic hepatitis C, as published in Intervirology in 2011. 22. Gu et al. evaluated the performance of HCV antigen or RNA kits for screening HCV-infected samples, as published in the Chinese Journal of Biologicals in 2014. 23. Van Helden and Weiskirchen reviewed the clinical evaluation of HCV core antigen determination for hepatitis C diagnostics, as published in Z Gastroenterology in 2014. 24. Schnuriger et al. investigated the early detection of HCV infection using a combined antigen-antibody detection assay, with potential applications in HIV co-infected individuals, as published in Pathology Biology in 2007. 25. Okazaki et al. developed a high-range method for detecting HCV markers, as published in Rinsho Byori in 2008. 26. Sidharthan et al. evaluated the utility of HCV viral load monitoring during direct-acting antiviral therapy, as published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2015. 27. Snijdewind et al. reviewed the current and future applications of dried blood spots in viral disease management, as published in Antiviral Research in 2012. 28. Grüner et al. described the preparation and processing of dried blood spots for use in immunoassays and molecular techniques, as published in the Journal of Visualized Experiments in 2015. 29. McDade et al. highlighted the use of dried blood spots as a minimally invasive method for integrating biomarkers into population-based research, as published in Demography in 2007. 30. Hirtz and Lehmann discussed the clinical revolution of using dried blood spots for blood sampling, as published in Annals of Clinical Biology in 2015. 31. Ross et al. evaluated the detection of HBV, HCV, and HIV infections using dried blood spots, focusing on the performance of the ARCHITECT system and other commercial assays, as published in Virology Journal in 2013. 32. Greenman et al. conducted a systematic review on the use of dried blood spots for HCV RNA genotyping, quantification, and storage, as published in the Journal of Viral Hepatitis in 2015. 33. Jones et al. reviewed the effectiveness of interventions to increase hepatitis C testing uptake among high-risk groups, as published in the European Journal of Public Health in 2014. 34. Boa-Sorte et al. evaluated dried blood spot testing for antenatal screening of HTLV, HIV, syphilis, toxoplasmosis, and hepatitis B and C, as published in the Brazilian Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2014. 35. Forbi et al. applied dried blood spot testing for serodiagnosis of HBV in a hyper-endemic nation, as published in Annals of African Medicine in 2010. 36. Kania et al. combined rapid diagnostic tests and dried blood spot assays for point-of-care testing of HIV, HBV, and HCV in Burkina Faso, as published in Clinical Microbiology and Infection in 2013. 37. Lee et al. evaluated the dried blood spot collection method for detecting HIV Ag/Ab, HBsAg, anti-HBs, and anti-HCV in a Malaysian tertiary referral hospital, as published in Annals of the Academy of Medicine Singapore in 2011. 38. Mendy et al. explored the use of dried blood spots for detecting HBV surface antigenemia and alpha-fetoprotein in field-based studies and clinical care in HBV-endemic areas, as published in the Journal of Viral Hepatitis in 2005. 39. Mohamed et al. assessed dried blood spot sampling for HBV serology and molecular testing, as published in PLoS One in 2013. 40. Villa et al. demonstrated the utility of dried blood spots for detecting HBV markers in epidemiological research, as published in the Journal of Clinical Pathology in 1981. 41. Villar et al. evaluated dried blood spots as a simple method for detecting HBV markers, as published in the Journal of Medical Virology in 2011. 42. Brandao et al. optimized commercial EIAs for HCV antibody detection in dried blood spots under various storage conditions, as published in the Journal of Medical Virology in 2012. 43. Waterboer et al. used dried blood spots for seroepidemiology of infections with HPV, H. pylori, HCV, and JC virus, as published in Cancer Epidemiology Biomarkers & Prevention in 2012. 44. Nandagopal et al. evaluated dried blood spots as an alternative specimen for diagnosing anti-HCV in resource-limited settings, as published in the Indian Journal of Medical Microbiology in 2014. 45. Dokubo et al. compared HCV RNA and antibody detection in dried blood spots and plasma specimens, as published in the Journal of Clinical Virology in 2014. 46. Tejada-Strop et al. reported disparate detection outcomes for anti-HCV IgG and HCV RNA in dried blood spots, as published in the Journal of Virological Methods in 2015. 47. Chevaliez et al. highlighted the potential of dried blood spots for large-scale HCV screening, diagnosis, and treatment monitoring, as presented at the International Liver Congress in 2014. 48. Parker et al. developed a method for detecting and confirming HCV antibodies in dried blood spots, as published in the Journal of Virological Methods in 1997. 49. Lukacs et al. conducted a feasibility study on simultaneous detection of HIV antibodies, HCV antibodies, and HBV antigens in dried blood spots using a multi-analyte immunoassay, as published in Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine in 2005. 50. McCarron et al. evaluated HCV antibody detection in dried blood spots, as published in the Journal of Viral Hepatitis in 1999. 51. Shepherd et al. developed an HCV avidity test for determining recent and past infections in plasma and dried blood spots, as published in the Journal of Clinical Virology in 2013. 52. Alidjinou et al. detected HBV infection markers in dried plasma spots among patients in Congo-Brazzaville, as published in Diagnostic Microbiology and Infectious Disease in 2014. 53. Alhusseini et al. demonstrated that HBV DNA can be amplified directly from dried blood spots on filter paper, as published in the American Journal of Biochemistry and Biotechnology in 2012. 54. Durgadevi et al. reviewed serological and molecular diagnosis of HBV, as published in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2012. 55. Gupta et al. directly detected HBV from dried blood spots using PCR amplification, as published in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology in 1992. 56. Halfon et al. presented findings on dried blood spots for HBV serology and molecular testing at the International Liver Congress in 2012.
